<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $T\in L(X)$ be invertible. Then $X$ has \textit{simultaneous zero inclusion property (in short, $S0I$)} at $T$ if $0\in W(T) \implies 0\in W(T^{-1})$. We say $X$ has \textit{$S0I$} if for each invertible $T\in L(X)$, $0\in W(T)\implies 0\in W(T^{-1}).$
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{BJ_James}
    Let $X$ be a normed space and let $x, y\in X.$ Then $x\perp_B y$ if and only if there exists $x^*\in J(x)$ such that $x^*(y)=0.$
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\cite{Day47, James47a}\label{symmetry}
Let $X$ be a Banach space with $\dim(X)\geq 3$. Then Birkhoff-James orthogonality is symmetric, i.e., for all $x, y\in X$, $x\perp_B \implies y\perp_B x$ if and only if the norm on $X$ is induced by an inner product.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{connection; Poon}
     A normed space $X$ has the $S0I$ property if and only if, for every invertible $A \in L(X),$  and $x\neq 0$
and $x\perp_B Ax$ implies there exists  $z \neq 0$ such that $Az\perp_B  z.$
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{main}
    Let $X$ be a smooth and ALUR normed space. Then  $X$ has the simultaneous zero inclusion property ($S0I$) if and only if Birkhoff-James orthogonality in $X$ is symmetric, i.e., for all $x, y\in X$, $x\perp_B y\implies y\perp_B x.$
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop1}
	    Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $T\in L(X)$ be invertible. Then $X$ has $S0I$ at $T$ if and only if either of the following holds true:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item [(i] $\mathcal{P}_T=\emptyset$ as well as $\mathcal{Q}_T=\emptyset.$
            \item[(ii)] Both $\mathcal{P}_T$ and $\mathcal{Q}_T$ are nonempty.  
        \end{itemize}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a Banach space. Then $X$ does not have $S0I$ if and only if there exists an invertible $T\in L(X)$ such that $\mathcal{P}_T\neq \emptyset$ but $\mathcal{Q}_T=\emptyset.$
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop; $S0I$}
        Let $T\in L(X)$ be invertible. Suppose that  either of the following holds true:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item [(i)] $\mathcal{P}_T\cap \mathcal{L}_X \neq \emptyset$;
            \item [(ii)] $\mathcal{Q}_T\cap \mathcal{R}_X\neq \emptyset$;
            \item[(iii)] $T(\mathcal{P}_T)\cap \mathcal{R}_{T(X)}\neq \emptyset$;
            \item[(iv)] $T(\mathcal{Q}_T)\cap \mathcal{L}_{T(X)}\neq \emptyset$.
        \end{itemize}
        Then $X$ has $S0I$ at $T.$ Consequently, if it holds for every invertible $T\in L(X)$ then $X$ has $S0I$.
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We only show (i) and (iii) as (ii) and (iv) follows similarly.\\
    (i) Suppose that $x\in \mathcal{P}_T\cap \mathcal{L}_X.$ Then $x\perp_B Tx$. Also, $x$ being left symmetric we have $Tx\perp_B x.$ This implies $\mathcal{P}_T\neq \emptyset$ as well as $\mathcal{Q}_T\neq\emptyset.$ Thus from Proposition \ref{prop1} we get $X$ has $S0I$ at $T.$  \\
    (iii) Let $y\in T(\mathcal{P}_T)\cap \mathcal{R}_{T(X)}.$ Then $y=Tx$ for some $x\in \mathcal{P}_T.$ Since $Tx$ is right symmetric,  $Tx\perp_B x$ and therefore, $\mathcal{Q}_T\neq \emptyset.$ This proves again from Proposition \ref{prop1} that $X$ has $S0I$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Let $X=\ell_p^3$ with $1<p<\infty$ and let $T\in L(\ell_p^3)$ be the following with respect to standard ordered basis:
    \[T=\begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 2 & 1\\
        1 & 1 & 0\\
        1 & 0 & 2
    \end{pmatrix}\]
    Clearly, $T$ is invertible. Since $Te_1 \in span\{e_2, e_3\},$ it follows that $e_1\perp_B Te_1.$ Moreover, from \cite{CSS} we have $e_1$ is a left symmetric point in $\ell_p^3$ Thus we have $e_1\in \mathcal{P}_T\cap \mathcal{L}_X.$ This implies from Proposition \ref{prop; $S0I$} that $X$ has $S0I$ at $T.$
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem; smooth and exposed}
   Let $x \in X$ be such that $x$ is smooth as well as exposed. If for any $v\in S_X,$  $J(x)\cap J(v)\neq \emptyset$ then $x=v.$
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{Dual; Radon}
    Let $X$ be a Radon plane then $X^*$ is also a Radon plane.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Suppose that $x^*\perp_B y^*$ for some $x^*,y^*\in S_{X^*}$. By Theorem \ref{BJ_James}, there exists $x\in S_X$ such that $|x^*(x)|=1,$ and   $y^*(x)=0.$ Choose $y\in S_X$ with $x^*(y)=0$. Since $x^*\in J(x)\cup J(-x)$, Theorem \ref{BJ_James} gives $x\perp_B y$. As $X$ is a Radon plane, $y\perp_B x$. Hence, again by Theorem \ref{BJ_James}, there exists $z^*\in J(y)$ such that $z^*(x)=0$. Since $y^*(x)=0$ and $y^*(y)=1$, we have $z^*=c  y^*$. Therefore, $y^*\perp_B x^*,$ and thus $X^*$ is a Radon plane.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{finite; smooth}
     Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional smooth or strictly convex Banach space. Then $X$ has $S0I$ if and only if Birkhoff-James orthogonality is symmetric in $X.$
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since the sufficient part follows from Theorem \ref{connection; Poon} directly, we show the necessary part.
As $X$ is smooth, we can use the arguments given in the proof of Theorem \ref{main} and obtain that there exists an open set $U$ of $S_X$ containing $K$ such that for all $v\in U$ $Re\, h(v)>0$. Also, $Re\, g(v)\geq 0$ for all $v\in U.$ Here only we need to show that  there exists $c>0$ such that $Re \, g(v)\geq c>0$ for all $v\in S_X\setminus U.$  As $S_X\setminus U$ is compact,  $Re\, g(v)>0$ for all $v\in S_X\setminus U$ and this implies there exists $c>0$ such that $c=\min_{v\in S_X\setminus U} Re\, g(v).$ Then we can construct the same $S_\lambda$ to prove the desired result.\\
On the other hand, if $X$ is  strictly convex then $X^*$ is smooth. As $X$ has $S0I$,  we note from \cite[Th. 2.2]{Bracic} that $X^*$ also has $S0I$. Following the above argument we get that Birkhoff-James orthogonality in $X^*$ is symmetric. If $X$ is complex Banach space then clearly, $X^*$ is a Hilbert space. Whereas, if we consider $X$ as real Banach space then
For $\dim X\geq 3$ we have $X^*$ is a Hilbert space and consequently, $X$ is also a Hilbert space. Thus Birkhoff-James orthogonality in $X$ is symmetric. If $\dim X=2$ then $X^*$ is a Radon plane and so is $X$ (see Lemma \ref{Dual; Radon}). This implies Birkhoff-James orthogonality is symmetric in $X.$
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a  Banach space with dimension more than two. Suppose that either of the following holds true:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item [(i)] $X$ is finite-dimensional smooth.
        \item[(ii)] $X$ is finite-dimensional strictly convex.
        \item[(ii)] $X$ is infinite-dimensional ALUR.
    \end{itemize}
    Then  $X$ has $S0I$ if and only if the norm of $X$ is induced by an inner product.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
This shows that, for $1<p<\infty$, the space $\ell_p^n$ has the $S0I$ property if and only if $p=2$. We recall that, in Remark 3.8 of \cite{Bracic}, the authors conjectured that $\ell_p^n$ does not have the $S0I$ property for $p\neq 2$. Our result confirms this conjecture and, moreover, extends it to the general setting of $L_p(\mu)$ spaces for $1<p<\infty$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemma; positive}
    Let $X$ be a real finite-dimensional polyhedral Banach space and let $T\in L(X)$. Suppose that $y^*(Tx)>0$ for all $(x, y^*)\in \Pi \cap ({\rm Ext}\, B_X \times {\rm Ext}\, B_{X^*}).$ Then for any $(v, v^*)\in \Pi$, $v^*(Tv)>0.$
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Fix $(v,v^*)\in \Pi$. Since $B_X$ is a  polyhedron, there exist $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \in {\rm Ext}\, B_X$ and $\alpha_i>0$, $\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i=1$, such that
$v=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i x_i.$ Since $v^*\in J(v)$, we have $1=v^{*}(v)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i v^{*}(x_i).$
As $v^{*}(x_i)\leq1$ for every $i$, it follows that
$v^{*}(x_i)=1,\, i\in \{1,\ldots,n\}.$ Hence $v^{*}\in J(x_i)$ for every $i$. Since $J(x_i)$ is a  face of $B_{X^*}$, we can write $ v^{*}=\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}\beta_{ij}y_{ij}^*,$
where $\beta_{ij}\geq0$, $\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}\beta_{ij}=1$, and  $y_{ij}^*\in{\rm Ext}\, J(x_i)\subseteq{\rm Ext}\, B_{X^*}.$ Therefore,
\begin{eqnarray*}
v^{*}(Tv)&=&v^{*}\left(T\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i x_i\right)\\
&=&\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i v^{*}(Tx_i)\\
&=&\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}\beta_{ij}y_{ij}^*(Tx_i).
\end{eqnarray*}
By the hypothesis, $y_{ij}^*(Tx_i)>0$ for every $i,j$. Since $\alpha_i,\beta_{ij}\geq0$ and $\sum_i\alpha_i=\sum_j\beta_{ij}=1$, we conclude that
$v^{*}(Tv)>0.$
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{polyhedral}
    Let $X$ be a real finite-dimensional polyhedral Banach space. Then $X$ has $S0I$ property if and only if Birkhoff-James orthogonality in $X$ is symmetric.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Since the sufficient part is trivial, we only prove the necessary part.  \\  Let ${\rm Ext}\, B_{X^*}=\{\pm y_1^*, \pm y_2^*, \ldots, \pm y_k^*\}.$ Suppose on the contrary there exists $x, y\in S_X$ such that $x\perp_B y$ but $y\not\perp_B x.$ Choose $y\in {\rm Sm}\,(X)\cap S_X.$ Indeed, consider $x\in {\rm Ext}\, B_X.$ Suppose that $y_k^*\in {\rm Ext}\, J(x).$ If we take a smooth point $y$ in the corresponding facet $F_k:=\{z\in S_X: y_k^*(z)=1\}$ then clearly, $y\not\perp_B x.$  Let $J(y)=\{y_1^*\}$ and consider the corresponding facet $F_{1}=\{z\in S_X: y_1^*(z)=1\}.$  We assume that $y_1^*(x)=a>0.$ Define $T_1=y^*\otimes x$ and $T_2=I- y^*\otimes y.$  Then we want to find a $\lambda$ such that for $S_\lambda=T_1+\lambda T_2$, $v^*S_\lambda v\neq 0$ for all $(v, v^*)\in \Pi.$ From Lemma \ref{lemma; positive} it is enough to show that $y_{jk}^*S_\lambda v_j$ has the same sign for each  $v_j\in {\rm Ext}\, B_X$ and $y_{jk}^*\in {\rm Ext}\, J(v_j).$ Let $$M=\max\{|y_{ij}^*T_1v_i|: v_i\in {\rm Ext}\, B_X, \, y_{ij}^*\in {\rm Ext}\,(J(v_i))\}$$ and let $$c=\inf\{|y_{ij}^*T_2v_i|: v_i\in {\rm Ext}\, B_X, \, y_{ij}^*\in {\rm Ext}\,(J(v_i))\setminus \{\pm y_1^*\}\}.$$ Clearly, $c>0.$ We choose $\lambda > M/c>0$. Since for each $v_i\in {\rm Ext}\, B_X\cap (F_1\cup -F_1),$ we obtain $y_1^*S_\lambda v_i= a>0.$ Also, for any $v_i\in {\rm Ext}\, B_X, \, y_{ij}^*\in {\rm Ext}\,(J(v_i))\setminus \{\pm y_1^*\},$ we have $$|y_{ij}^*T_1v_i|\leq M = \frac{M}{c} c< \lambda |y_{ij}^*T_2v_i|.$$ This implies for any $v_i\in {\rm Ext}\, B_X, \, y_{ij}^*\in {\rm Ext}\,(J(v_i)),$ $y_{ij}^*S_\lambda v_i>0.$ This proves that for any $(v, v^*)\in \Pi$ we get $v^*S_\lambda  v\neq 0.$ Also, following the same argument as given in the proof of Theorem \ref{main} that $S_\lambda $ is invertible and considering $T=S_\lambda^{-1}$ we arrive at our desired result.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{cor; two-dim}
     Let $X$ be a real two-dimensional Banach space. If either of the following holds true
     \begin{itemize}
         \item [(i)] $X$ is smooth.
         \item[(ii)] $X$ is strictly convex.
         \item[(iii)] $X$ is polyhedral space.
     \end{itemize}
     Then $X$ has $S0I$ if and only if $X$ must be a Radon plane. Moreover, if we consider the scalar field is complex and $X$ is smooth or strictly convex, then $X$ has $S0I$ implies Birkhoff-James orthogonality is symmetric.
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{Mazur}
     Suppose that $X$ is a  two-dimensional Banach space and let $x_1, x_2\in S_X$ such that $x_1\neq \pm x_2.$  Consider the following set: $$K=\bigg\{\frac{(1-t)x_1+tx_2}{\|(1-t)x_1+tx_2\|}: 0\leq t\leq 1\bigg\}.$$ Then ${\rm Sm}\,(X)\cap K$ is dense in $K.$
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a two-dimensional real Banach space. Then $X$ has $S0I$ if and only if $X$ is a Radon plane.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Since the sufficient part is clear, we only show that necessary part.\\
   If $X$ is smooth then it directly  follows from Corollary \ref{cor; two-dim}. So  assume that $X$ is nonsmooth. Suppose on the contrary that $X$ is not a Radon plane. Since every left symmetric element of $X$ is smooth,  We may consider $x\in {\rm Ext}\, B_X \setminus {\rm Sm}\, (X)$ such that there exists $y\in S_X$ with $x\perp_By$ but $y\not\perp_B x$ with $y^*(x)=a>0.$  We  can choose $y\in {\rm Sm}\, (X)\cap S_X.$ Indeed, One can easily check that the set  $A_x\cap x^\perp$ is open in $x^\perp$ with respect to the subspace topology. Now by Mazur's theorem we have smooth points are dense in $X$ and consequently from Lemma \ref{Mazur}, there exists $y\in A_x\cap x^\perp$ with $y\in {\rm Sm}\, (X)\cap S_X.$    Consider  $T_1=y^*\otimes x$ and $T_2=I- y^*\otimes y.$  Let $\mathcal Z(T_2):=\{(v, v^*)\in \Pi: v^*T_2v=0\}.$   Now we proceed with the following two cases.\\
    \textbf{Case-I:} Suppose that $y$ is exposed. Observe that $\mathcal Z(T_2)=\{\pm(y, y^*)\in \Pi: J(y)=\{y^*\}\}.$ At $\pm (y, y^*),$ $y^*T_1y=y^*(x)=a>0.$ Also, for $T\in L(X)$, the map $\phi_T: \Pi\to \mathbb R$ defined by $\phi_T(x, x^*)=x^*Tx$ is continuous. Thus there exists a open set of $V=U\times U^* \subset \Pi$ with respect to product topology containing $\mathcal{Z}(T_2)$ such that for all $(v, v^*)\in V\cup (-V)$, $v^*T_1v>0.$ Moreover, for all $(v, v^*)\in \Pi \setminus V,$ we take $\inf |v^*T_2v|=c>0$ and $\sup |v^*T_1v|\leq M.$ Considering $\lambda > M/c>0$ and $S_\lambda=T_1+\lambda T_2$  we proceed with the same argument as given in the main theorem to obtain  $v^*S_\lambda v \neq 0$ for all $(v, v^*)\in \Pi.$\\
    \textbf{Case-II:} Now suppose that $y$ is not exposed. Since $y\in {\rm Sm}\, (X)$ this implies there exists $v_1, v_2\in S_X$ such that $y=(1-t)v_1 + t v_2$ for some $0<t<1.$ Note that  $$\mathcal{Z}(T_2)=\{\pm(v, y^*): v\in F_{y^*}, J(y)=\{y^*\}\},$$ where $F_{y^*}=\{(1-t)v_1+tv_2: 0\leq t\leq 1\}.$ For $(v, y^*)\in \mathcal{Z}(T_2),$ $y^*T_1v=a>0.$  For each $v\in F_{y^*}$  there exists an open neighbourhood $U^*$ of  $y^*$ such that for all $z^*\in U^*$ and $(v, z^*)\in  \Pi,$ $z^*T_1v>0.$ Also, $z^*T_2v\geq0.$ On the other hand, note that the set $$K=\Pi \setminus \{(u, u^*): u=(1-t)v_1+tv_2, 0<t<1 \,\, \mbox{and}\,\, u^*\in U^*\}$$ is a compact set and therefore, for any $(v, v^*)\in \Pi \setminus K$ we may consider $\min |v^*T_2v|=c>0.$  Then taking $\lambda> \frac{\max|v^*T_1v|}{c}>0$ and $S_\lambda=T_1+\lambda T_2$ we get $v^*S_\lambda v \neq 0$ for all $(v, v^*)\in \Pi.$ Therefore, for $T=S_{\lambda}^{-1},$ we get $x\perp_B Tx$ whereas, $v\not\perp_B T^{-1}v$ for all $v\in S_X.$ This contradicts that $X$ has $S0I$.  Hence the theorem.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional real Banach space and let $T$ be invertible. Suppose that $I\perp_B T\implies T\perp_B I.$ Then $X$ has $S0I$ at $T.$
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
From norm derivatives, given $T, A\in L(X)$ we have the following functions:
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        \rho'_\pm(T, A)= \|T\|\lim_{t\to^{0\pm}} \frac{\|T+tA\|-\|T\|}{t}.
    \end{eqnarray*}
    From \cite{Wojcik}, we note that this can be written as: $\rho'_+(T, A)=\sup\{\rho'_+(Tx, Ax): x\in M_T\cap {\rm Ext}\, B_X\}$ and $\rho'_-(T, A)=\inf\{\rho'_-(Tx, Ax): x\in M_T\cap {\rm Ext}\, B_X\}.$ In our case we consider $A=I$ and denote $\rho'_+(T, I)=\rho_+$ and $\rho'_-(T, I)=\rho'_-.$  Suppose that $0\in W(T)$ and therefore, there exists $x\in S_X$ such that $x\perp_B Tx$ which implies that $I\perp_B T$ (see \cite{Bhatia}). Now following our hypothesis we have $T\perp_B I.$ This yields $\rho'_-\leq 0\leq \rho'_+.$ Since $S_X$ is  compact, there exists $x_0, y_0\in M_T\cap {\rm Ext}\, B_X$ and $u^*\in J(Tx_0), v^*\in J(Ty_0)$ such that $\rho'_+=u^*(x_0)$ and $\rho'_-=v^*(y_0),$ respectively. We note the following two cases:\\
    \textbf{Case-I:} Suppose that $\rho'_+=0$. Then $u^*(x_0)=0$. This implies $Tx_0\perp_B x_0.$ Similarly, if $\rho'_-=0$ we have $Ty_0\perp_B y_0.$ From Proposition \ref{prop1} we conclude that $X$ has $S0I$ at $T.$\\
    \textbf{Case-II:} Now suppose that $\rho'_-<0<\rho'_+.$ For each $x\in S_X$, we define the following two functions $h_+, h_-: S_X\to \mathbb{R}$ such that:
    \begin{eqnarray*}
        h_+(x)=\max_{y^*\in J(Tx)} y^*(x)\\
        h_-(x)= \min_{y^*\in J(Tx)} y^*(x).
    \end{eqnarray*}
    It is easy to see that for $h_-\leq h_+$. Also, $h_-(y_0)=\rho'_-$ and $h_+(x_0)=\rho'_+.$ We next show that the function $h_+$ is upper semi-continuous whereas $h_-$ is lower semi-continuous. We only show it for $h_+$ as the case for $h_-$ follows similarly. Suppose that there exists $\{x_n\}\subset S_X$ such that $x_n\to x.$ Since for each $n\in \mathbb{N},$ $J(Tx_n)$ is a compact set. Thus there exists $y_n^*\in J(Tx_n)$ such that $h_+(x_n)=y_n^*(x_n)$ for each $n.$ Let $y_n^*\to y^*$ for some $y^*\in S_{X^*}.$ A straightforward computation shows that $y^*\in J(Tx)$ and $y^*(x)\leq h_+(x).$ So it follows that $\lim \sup h_+(x_n)\leq h_+(x).$ This proves our claim. \\
     \textit{Subcase-I:} If $x_0=y_0$ then we have $h_+(x_0)=\rho'_+\geq 0$ and $h_-(x_0)=\rho'_-\leq 0.$ Since $J(Tx_0)$ is compact convex subset of $S_{X^*},$ there exists $h\in J(Tx_0)$ such that $h(x_0)=0.$ This shows that $Tx_0\perp_B x_0.$ \\
     \textit{Subcase-II:} Suppose that $x_0 \neq y_0.$ We have the following possibilities:
     \[
     (i) h_+(y_0)\geq 0. (ii) h_-(x_0)> 0.  (iii) h_-(x_0)\leq 0 \,\,\mbox{and},\,\, (iv) h_+(y_0)<  0.
    \]
     If we consider Possibility (i) with $h_-(y_0)\leq 0,$ we get $w^*(y_0)\geq 0$ and $z^*(y_0)\leq0$. By convexity of $J(Ty_0),$ we have $y^*\in J(Ty_0)$ such that $y^*(y_0)=0.$ This implies $Ty_0\perp_B y_0.$ Similarly,  for possibility-(iii) we observe that $Tx_0\perp_B x_0.$ So let us assume that we have Possibility-(ii), i.e., $h_-(x_0) > 0$. Let $\gamma:[0, 1]\to S_X$ be a path defined as $\gamma(0)=x_0$ and $\gamma(1)=y_0.$ Let $S:=\{t\in [0, 1]: h_-(\gamma(t))\leq 0 \}.$ Note that $S\neq \emptyset$ as $t=1\in S.$ Assume that $t_0=\inf S.$ For all $t<t_0$ we have $h_-(\gamma(t))>0.$ Observe that $t_0>0.$ Indeed, if possible let $\exists \{t_n\}\in [0, 1]$ such that $t_n\to 0$ and $h_-(\gamma(t_n))\leq 0$ for each $n.$ Since $\gamma $ is continuous $\gamma(t_n)\to \gamma (0)=x_0.$ By lower semi-continuity of $h_-$ we have $h_-(x_0)\leq \lim\inf h_-(\gamma(t_n))\leq 0.$ This contradicts $h_-(x_0)>0.$ Thus we have $t_0>0.$ Also, since $t_0=\inf S,$ one can observe that $h_-(\gamma(t_0))\leq 0.$ On the other hand, consider  $\{s_n\}\in [0, 1]$ such that $s_n< t_0$ and $s_n\to t_0.$ Then $\gamma(s_n)\to \gamma(t_0)$ and $h_+(\gamma(s_n))\geq h_-(\gamma(s_n))>0$ for each $n.$ Since $h_+$ is upper semi-continuous, it follows that $h_+(\gamma(t_0))\geq \lim\sup h_+(\gamma(s_n)) \geq 0.$ This shows that there exists $t_0\in [0, 1]$ such that $h_+(\gamma(t_0))\geq 0$ whereas $h_-(\gamma(t_0))\leq 0.$ Let $\gamma(t_0)=z_0.$ Therefore, again using the fact that $J(Tz_0)$ is a convex subset of $S_{X^*}$, there exists $ h\in J(Tz_0)$  such that $h(z_0)=0.$ This implies $z_0\perp_B Tz_0.$ This proves that $X$ has $S0I$ at $T$ and  completes the theorem.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional real Banach space and let $T\in GL(X)$ be right symmetric. Then $X$ has $S0I$ at $T.$  Moreover, if $X=\ell_1^n$ then any extreme contraction in $L(X)$ has $S0I$.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
Of course, there exist operators that possess the $S0I$ property without being right symmetric. For instance, any invertible bounded linear operator on a Hilbert space that is not an isometry is not right symmetric (see \cite{Turnsek}), while it does possess the $S0I$ property. Although our theorem  tells that we only need right symmetry of $T$ with respect to $I$ to have $S0I$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
Suppose that $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite-dimensional unital real $C^*$ algebra and let $\mathcal{A}_+$ be the positive cone of $\mathcal{A}.$ Then for each invertible $A\in \mathcal{A}_+$, $\mathcal{A}$ has $S0I$ at $A.$
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
Let $X$ be a finite-dimensional real Banach space  and let $T\in L(X)$ be invertible. If the identity operator is local-$GL(X)$ left symmetric then $X$ has $S0I$.
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Let $X$ be the real three dimensional Euclidean space and let $T\in L(X)$ be the following matrix with respect to standard ordered basis of $X,$
    \[T=\begin{pmatrix}
        0 & 0 & 1\\
        0 & 2 & 0\\
        1 & 0 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}.\] Clearly, $T$ is invertible. Hence $X$ has $S0I$ at $T$. Moreover, it is easy to see that $M_T=\{\pm e_2\}.$ First note that $e_1\perp_B Te_1$ and this implies $I\perp_B T,$ whereas $Te_2= 2e_2$ implies that $Te_2\not\perp_B e_2$ and thus $T\not\perp_B I.$
<!-- end example-2 -->
